**Indore** (; [ISO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISO_15919 "ISO 15919"): _Indaura_, Hindi:[[ɪn̪d̪ɔːr]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Hindi_and_Urdu "Help:IPA/Hindi and Urdu")) is the largest city of the [Indian state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_state_and_union_territory_capitals_in_India "List of state and union territory capitals in India") of [Madhya Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madhya_Pradesh "Madhya Pradesh") where it serves as the [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_state_and_union_territory_capitals_in_India "List of state and union territory capitals in India") and the administrative headquarters of the eponymous [district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore_district "Indore district") and [division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore_division "Indore division").

Modern-day Indore was established on the banks of the [Kanh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kanh_River "Kanh River") and [Saraswati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saraswati_River_(Madhya_Pradesh) "Saraswati River (Madhya Pradesh)") rivers and traces its roots to its 16th-century founding as a trading hub between the [Deccan Plateau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_Plateau "Deccan Plateau") and [Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi "Delhi").[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-12) Following the conquest of [Malwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malwa "Malwa") by [Peshwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peshwa "Peshwa")[Baji Rao I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baji_Rao_I "Baji Rao I"), the city came under the control of the [Maratha Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maratha_Confederacy "Maratha Confederacy") until its annexation by the [British East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_East_India_Company "British East India Company").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-14) Prior to [Indian independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement "Indian independence movement"), [the Kingdom of Indore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore_State "Indore State") was a nineteen [Gun Salute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salute_state "Salute state")[Princely State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_State "Princely State") of the [British Raj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") with the [Holkars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Holkar "House of Holkar") as rulers.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-15)

With an estimated population of 5.6 million in 2025 distributed over nearly 10 thousand square kilometres, the metropolitan region encompassing Indore, [Ujjain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ujjain "Ujjain"), [Dewas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewas "Dewas"), [Pithampur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pithampur "Pithampur") and [Nagda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagda "Nagda") serves as the financial capital of Madhya Pradesh. One of India's main industrial hubs, the metropolitan region is a major center for pharmaceutical and automotive manufacturing with, notably, [Asia’s longest test track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATRAX "NATRAX").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-17)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-18)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-:6-20)

The largest education hub in central India, it is home to an [Indian Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Institute_of_Technology_Indore "Indian Institute of Technology Indore") and an [Indian Institute of Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Institute_of_Management_Indore "Indian Institute of Management Indore") and is one of the cities selected under the [central government's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_India "Government of India") flagship [Smart Cities Mission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smart_Cities_Mission "Smart Cities Mission") and [Swachh Survekshan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swachh_Survekshan "Swachh Survekshan") programmes.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-21)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-22)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-24)
Consistently ranked as India's [cleanest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cleanest_cities_in_India "List of cleanest cities in India"), Indore is regularly commended for its clean air and proper waste management.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-26)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-30)

## Etymology
[Gupta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire "Gupta Empire") inscriptions name Indore as "Indrapura".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-auto1-31) It is believed that the city is named after its Indreshwar Mahadev Temple, where [Shiva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shiva "Shiva") is the presiding deity.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-32)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-33) It is believed that [Indra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indra "Indra") himself did _[Tapasya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tapas\_(Indian\_religions) "Tapas (Indian religions)")_ (meditation) in this place and led sage Swami Indrapuri to establish the temple. Later, [Tukoji Rao Holkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tukoji_Rao_Holkar "Tukoji Rao Holkar") who belonged to the Holkar clan of the Marathas and was the feudatory of Indore, renovated the temple.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-34) The older name of Indore is believed to be **Indur**, as referenced in historical records.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-35) In 2017, a proposal was brought forward by the Indore Municipal Corporation to rename the city as "Indur".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-37)

## History
### Gupta Empire (Gupta era)
[Gupta Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire "Gupta Empire") inscription mentions Indore as city/town of Indrapura in Gupta Indore Copper plate inscription dated 146 Gupta era or 465 CE.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-38) These are also some of the earliest mentions of Indore where the city is mentioned as 'Indrapura'.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-39) Indrapura (modern day Indore) was then known for its sun temple, where in 464–65 CE, Gupta king [Skandagupta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skandagupta "Skandagupta") had made an endowment for the permanent maintenance of the city's sun temple. The temple was constructed by two merchants of the city – Achalavarman and Bhṛikuṇṭhasiṁha.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-auto1-31)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-40)
[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/02/466_CE_Indore_Copper_Plate_Inscription%2C_Hinduism%2C_Skandagupta%2C_Sanskrit.jpg/250px-466_CE_Indore_Copper_Plate_Inscription%2C_Hinduism%2C_Skandagupta%2C_Sanskrit.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:466_CE_Indore_Copper_Plate_Inscription,_Hinduism,_Skandagupta,_Sanskrit.jpg)
An early Gupta era inscription from ancient India. This is a photograph of a personal copy of plates published by John Fleet in 1888, with Inscriptions of the Early Gupta Kings And Their Successors, as a part of the Corpus Inscriptionum Indicarum series, Vol. 3

## History
### Holkar era (Maratha Empire)
During the [Mughal era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire"), the area under the modern Indore district was equally divided between the administrations (_[sarkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarkar\_(administrative\_division) "Sarkar (administrative division)")_ s) of [Ujjain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ujjain "Ujjain") and [Mandu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mandu,_Madhya_Pradesh "Mandu, Madhya Pradesh"). Kampel was the headquarters of a _mahal_ (administrative unit) under the Ujjain _sarkar_ of [Malwa Subah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malwa_Subah "Malwa Subah") (province). The area of the modern Indore city was included in the [Kampel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampel,_Indore "Kampel, Indore")[pargana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pargana "Pargana") (administrative unit).[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indore#cite_note-gazetteer_1971-41)

Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]

After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

Thambiran Vanakkam was printed at Kollam, the capital of Venad in 1578, during the Portuguese Era. It holds the record of the first book printed in any Indian language. It was written in the language Lingua Malabar Tamul which was spoken in Kerala during the medieval period.

In the early 18th century CE, the Travancore royal family adopted some members from the royal family of Kolathunadu based at Kannur.[48] Then, Marthanda Varma who inherited the Kingdom of Venad expanded the kingdom by conquering the kingdoms of Kayamkulam, Kottarakkara, Kottayam, Changanassery, Meenachil, Poonjar and Ambalappuzha.[49] In 1729, Marthanda Varma founded the princely state of Thiruvithamkoor and Thiruvananthapuram was made the capital in 1795 after shifting the capital from Padmanabhapuram in Kanyakumari district.[50] Thiruvananthapuram became a prominent city in Kerala under Marthanda Varma.[51]

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

Varma was born on 29 April 1848, as [M. R. Ry.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maha_Raja_Rajya_Shri "Maha Raja Rajya Shri") Ravi Varma ([Malayalam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayalam_language "Malayalam language"): രവി വർമ്മ), [Koil Thampuran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koyi_Thampuran "Koyi Thampuran") of Kilimanoor at [Kilimanoor palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilimanoor_palace "Kilimanoor palace") in the erstwhile [princely state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princely_state "Princely state") of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") (present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala"))[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-pal-6) into an aristocratic family that for over 200 years produced consorts for the princesses of the matrilineal Travancore royal family. His mother Uma Ambabayi Thampuratty belonged to the baronial family which ruled the Kilimanoor [feudal estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") within the kingdom of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore"). She was a poet and writer, and her work _Parvati Swayamvaram_ was published by Varma after her death. Ravi Varma's father was a scholar of [Sanskrit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanskrit "Sanskrit") and [Ayurveda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayurveda "Ayurveda") and hailed from the [Ernakulam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernakulam "Ernakulam") district in Kerala. Ravi Varma had two siblings, a sister named [Mangala Bayi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mangala_Bayi "Mangala Bayi") and a brother named [Raja Varma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C._Raja_Raja_Varma "C. Raja Raja Varma") (born 1860). The last-named was also a painter and worked closely with Ravi Varma all his life.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 1866, at age 18, Varma was married to 12-year-old Bhageerthi Bayi (known formally as Pooruruttati Nal Bhageerathi Bayi Thampuratty) of the royal house of [Mavelikkara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mavelikkara "Mavelikkara"), another major [fief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fief "Fief") of Travancore kingdom. Notably, the house of Mavellikara was a branch of the Royal House of Travancore. Bhageerthi was the youngest of three sisters; her two elder siblings were adopted into the royal family of Travancore in 1857 to perpetuate the lineage. Designated the Senior and Junior Rani of Attingal, their descendants were vested with the succession to the throne of Travancore. Therefore, Ravi Varma's connection to the royal family became very close due to his marriage with Bhageerthi. His children would be royal by birth, since they belonged to their mother's family. The marriage, which was arranged by the parents in the proper Indian manner, was considered successful. The couple had five children, two sons, and three daughters. Their elder son, Kerala Varma (b.1876) was of an excessively spiritual temperament. He never married and eventually renounced the world, leaving home for good in 1912. The younger son, Rama Varma (born 1879), inherited his father's artistic talent and studied at the [JJ School of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JJ_School_of_Arts "JJ School of Arts"), [Mumbai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumbai "Mumbai"). He was married to Gowri Kunjamma, sister of [Dewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dewan "Dewan")[PGN Unnithan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PGN_Unnithan "PGN Unnithan"), and became the father of seven children.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]

Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit

The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram  
See also: Merger of Kanyakumari with Madras State  
Painting by Raja Ravi Varma depicting Richard Temple-Grenville, 3rd Duke of Buckingham and Chandos being greeted by Visakham Thirunal, with Ayilyam Thirunal of Travancore looking on, during Buckingham's visit to Thiruvananthapuram in early 1880

Pre-historic periodedit

Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]
A map of Malabar Coast drawn by Homann Heirs in 1733. At that time, Travancore was only a small territory wedged between Kollam and Kanyakumari, as shown in the map (Present-day districts of Thiruvananthapuram and Kanyakumari only).  
Early Modern periodedit

Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit

The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]
Tourismedit  
Main article: Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram  
Harvesting lotus leaves from Vellayani Lake.
Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. [citation needed]

The main museums include the Kerala Science and Technology Museum (with its attached Priyadarsini Planetarium), the Napier Museum, the Kerala Soil Museum and the Koyikkal Palace Museum. Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is listed in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.[141]
Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]

Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]
16th IFFK 2011 banner at Kairali Theater Complex

The Malayalam film Industry was started in Thiruvananthapuram. The first Malayalam feature film, Vigathakumaran, directed by J. C. Daniel, was released in Thiruvananthapuram.[155] J. C. Daniel is considered the father of the Malayalam film industry. He also established the first film studio in Kerala, the Travancore National Pictures at Thiruvananthapuram in 1926.[156][157] The International Film Festival of Kerala (IFFK), which is held every year in December, is one of Asia's largest film festivals in terms of viewer participation.[158][159] In addition to various film festivals, the presence of the Central Board of Film Certification's regional office, many movie studios and production facilities like the Uma Studio, Chitranjali Studio, Merryland Studio, Kinfra Film and Video Park and Vismayas Max contribute to the growth of Thiruvananthapuram as a centre of cinema.[160][161]
Apart from the famous Padmanabhaswamy Temple, the city's architecture is championed by the Napier Museum and Thiruvananthapuram Zoo, one of the oldest zoos in India.[162] Other architectural landmarks include Kuthira Malika Palace, Kowdiar Palace, Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, Beemapally Mosque, Connemara Market, and the Mateer Memorial Church. Thiruvananthapuram was the main centre of Laurie Baker's architecture.[163]

**Raja Ravi Varma** (Malayalam:[[ɾaːd͡ʒaː ɾɐʋi ʋɐrmːɐ]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/Malayalam "Help:IPA/Malayalam")) (29 April 1848 – 2 October 1906[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-4)) was an Indian painter. His works are one of the best examples of the fusion of European [academic art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_art "Academic art") with a purely Indian sensibility and iconography. He greatly enhanced his reach and influence as a painter and public figure by making affordable [lithographs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lithography "Lithography") of his paintings available to the public. His lithographs increased the involvement of common people with fine arts and defined artistic tastes. His religious depictions of Hindu deities and works from [Indian epic poetry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") and [Puranas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puranas "Puranas") have received critical acclaim. He was part of the royal family of [Parappanad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parappanad "Parappanad"), [Malappuram district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malappuram_district "Malappuram district").
Raja Ravi Varma was closely related to the royal family of [Travancore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Travancore "Travancore") of present-day [Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala "Kerala") state in India. Later in his life, two of his granddaughters were adopted into the royal family.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raja_Ravi_Varma#cite_note-5)

texts.2: Thiruvananthapuram (Malayalam pronunciation: [t̪iɾuʋənən̪d̪ɐˈbuɾəm] ⓘ tirr-ROO-və-nun-Tə-poor-əm), also known as Trivandrum, is the capital city of the Indian state of Kerala.[9][10] As of 2011, the Thiruvananthapuram Municipal Corporation had a population of 957,730 over an area of 214.86 km2,[11] making it the most populous city in Kerala.[12] The larger Thiruvananthapuram metropolitan area has over 1.7 million inhabitants within an area of 543 km2, making it the second-most populous metropolitan area in Kerala after Kochi.[13]. Thiruvananthapuram is one of the few cities in India that serves as a state capital and is also centre for heritage, maritime activities, information technology, research and development, space research, defence, automotive technology, and biosciences. It is also among the few cities in the world where both an international airport and an international seaport are located within the city in close proximity to the city centre.[14]
texts.3:

Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]
texts.4:
Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit
texts.5:
The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name. [citation needed]
Historyedit  
Main article: History of Thiruvananthapuram

Pre-historic periodedit
texts.6:
Thiruvananthapuram is a relatively modern region with trading traditions dating back to 1000 BCE.[33][34] It is believed that the ships of King Solomon landed in a port then called Ophir (now Poovar) in Thiruvananthapuram in 1036 BCE.[35][36] The city was the trading post for spices, sandalwood and ivory.[37] However, the ancient political and cultural history of the city was almost entirely independent from that of the rest of Kerala. [citation needed]
Ancient periodedit
The southern region of present-day Kerala state (The coastal belt between Thiruvananthapuram and Alappuzha) was under the Ay dynasty, which was more related to the Pandya dynasty of Madurai.[38][page needed] The early rulers of the city were the Ays. Vizhinjam, which is now a region in present-day Thiruvananthapuram, was the capital of the Ay dynasty.[39] Vizhinjam was an important port city from as early as the second century BC.[40][41] During the Ay dynasty's rule, Thiruvananthapuram witnessed many battles in which the Chola and Pandyan dynasties attempted to capture the port town.[42][43]
Middle Agesedit
After the death of king Vikramaditya Varaguna in 925 AD, the glory of the Ays departed and almost all their territories became part of the Chera dynasty.[44][19] During the tenth century, the Cholas attacked and sacked Vizhinjam and surrounding regions.[19] The port in Vizhinjam and the historic education centre of Kanthalloor Sala were also destroyed by Cholas during this period.[45][46] A branch of the Ay family, which had controlled the Padmanabhaswamy Temple, merged with the Kingdom of Venad in the 12th century.[19]

Early Modern periodedit
texts.24:
Tourism is a significant economic sector.[127][128][129] The presence of natural attractions like beaches, backwaters, hills, and plantations and attractions like heritage, history, Ayurveda, medical tourism and knowledge centres attract many tourists.[130] The city experienced a surge of investment in the real estate, infrastructure and retail sectors in 2016–17.[131]
Port-based developmentedit
Thiruvananthapuram is a commercial port city with port-related infrastructure due to the presence of the Deepwater Container Transhipment port operated by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram.[132]
The port is located close to international shipping routes, approximately 10 to 12 nautical miles (19 to 22 km) from the busy Persian Gulf–Malacca shipping lane.[133] It has a natural depth of 18 to 20 metres (59 to 66 ft), enabling it to accommodate large container vessels.[134] The berths are designed to handle vessels of up to 24,000 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU).[135] Port-related development has been associated with increased activity in logistics, warehousing, shipping services and supporting infrastructure, trade and transport connectivity.[citation needed]
Trivandrum Outer Ring Roadedit
texts.25:
The proposed Trivandrum Outer Ring Road (ORR) (ORR), also known as the Outer Area Growth Corridor (OAGC), is a major infrastructure initiative aimed at supporting the long-term economic development of the city and its surrounding region. The corridor, extending approximately 78–80 km between Vizhinjam International Seaport Thiruvananthapuram and Navaikulam, is planned as a six-lane access-controlled highway with designated economic zones along its alignment. The TOAGC master plan envisages the development of multiple sector-specific clusters, including logistics, industrial development, information technology, healthcare, health tourism, general tourism, education, and commercial services, forming an integrated investment region around the capital area. Key nodes such as Vizhinjam, Kovalam, Vembayam, Mangalapuram, and Nedumangad have been identified for focused development, including a logistics hub at Vizhinjam and a health and tourism hub in the coastal belt. The project is also expected to strengthen connectivity between Vizhinjam International Seaport, the IT corridors, and the national highway network, thereby facilitating port-led industrial growth and regional economic expansion.[136][137][138]
Tourismedit  
Main article: Tourism in Thiruvananthapuram  
Harvesting lotus leaves from Vellayani Lake.
Thiruvananthapuram is a major tourist hub in India.[128] Kovalam and Varkala are popular beach towns near the city.[139] Other important beaches include Poovar, Shankumugham Beach, Azhimala Beach, Vizhinjam Beach and Veli Beach. Other places of interest include the Agasthyamala rain forests, Neyyar Wildlife Sanctuary, Kallar, Braemore, Ponmudi hills, Poovar, the Anchuthengu backwaters, Varkala Cliffs and Kappil-Edava lakes. [citation needed]
The city is also known for its unique style of architecture involving Kerala Architecture with British and Dravidian influences.[140] Napier museum, Thiruvanathapuram Zoo, Padmanabha Swamy temple, Kuthira Malika palace, Kilimanoor palace and The Thiruvananthapuram Golf Club heritage building are examples of this. [citation needed]
texts.26:
The main museums include the Kerala Science and Technology Museum (with its attached Priyadarsini Planetarium), the Napier Museum, the Kerala Soil Museum and the Koyikkal Palace Museum. Agasthyamala Biosphere Reserve is listed in UNESCO's World Network of Biosphere Reserves.[141]
Cultureedit  
Main article: Culture of Thiruvananthapuram  
Established in 1855, the Napier Museum contains a vast collection of Ancient paintings and archaeological artefacts
Thiruvananthapuram is known as the "Evergreen City of India" because of its green landscapes and the presence of many public parks.[142] Thiruvananthapuram has historically been a cultural hub in Southern India due to the development of arts, architecture and liberal customs by the rulers of erstwhile Thiruvananthapuram. As a testimony to this, renowned artists like Maharaja Swathi Thirunal and Raja Ravi Varma hail from the city.[143][144] Prominent social reformers such as Sri Narayana Guru, Chattampi Swamikal, Ayyankali, Vakkom Moulavi and C. V. Raman Pillai also are from Thiruvananthapuram.[145]
texts.27:
Two of the three Malayalam triumvirate poets, Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer and Kumaran Asan are from Thiruvananthapuram.[146][147] Annual literature festivals like the Kovalam Literary Festival, are held in the city.[148] Literary development is further aided by state institutions such as the State Central Library, one of the oldest public libraries in India, which was established in 1829,[149] and other major libraries including the Thiruvananthapuram Corporation Central library, and the Kerala University Library.[150] Thiruvananthapuram has been a hub of classical music since the days of Maharaja of Travancore, Swathi Thirunal.[151][152] Thiruvananthapuram is known for many music festivals like the Navarathri Music Festival, one of the oldest festivals of its kind in South India,[151] Swathi Sangeethotsavam, Soorya Music fest, Neelakanta Sivan Music Fest and many other music festivals are organised by various cultural groups.[151] The 111-day-long Soorya Festival is the biggest art and cultural event in Kerala.[153][154] The Soorya Festival features film festivals, theatre festivals, dance, music, painting and photography exhibitions.[153]
16th IFFK 2011 banner at Kairali Theater Complex
texts.28:
The Malayalam film Industry was started in Thiruvananthapuram. The first Malayalam feature film, Vigathakumaran, directed by J. C. Daniel, was released in Thiruvananthapuram.[155] J. C. Daniel is considered the father of the Malayalam film industry. He also established the first film studio in Kerala, the Travancore National Pictures at Thiruvananthapuram in 1926.[156][157] The International Film Festival of Kerala (IFFK), which is held every year in December, is one of Asia's largest film festivals in terms of viewer participation.[158][159] In addition to various film festivals, the presence of the Central Board of Film Certification's regional office, many movie studios and production facilities like the Uma Studio, Chitranjali Studio, Merryland Studio, Kinfra Film and Video Park and Vismayas Max contribute to the growth of Thiruvananthapuram as a centre of cinema.[160][161]
Apart from the famous Padmanabhaswamy Temple, the city's architecture is championed by the Napier Museum and Thiruvananthapuram Zoo, one of the oldest zoos in India.[162] Other architectural landmarks include Kuthira Malika Palace, Kowdiar Palace, Attukal Bhagavathy Temple, Beemapally Mosque, Connemara Market, and the Mateer Memorial Church. Thiruvananthapuram was the main centre of Laurie Baker's architecture.[163]

Located on the west coast of India near the extreme south of the mainland, Thiruvananthapuram is a port city located 10 nautical miles (19 km; 12 mi)[15] from a heavily trafficked east–west shipping channel. The city is home to India's first deep-water trans-shipment port, owned by the Vizhinjam International Seaport Ltd. Thiruvananthapuram under the Government of Kerala.[16] The city is characterised by its undulating terrain of low coastal hills.[17] Thiruvananthapuram is also known for its cultural heritage, being associated with the musical contributions of Swathi Thirunal Rama Varma and the artistic legacy of painter Raja Ravi Varma. Thiruvananthapuram has contributed to the development of Malayalam literature through individuals like Ulloor S. Parameswara Iyer, Kumaran Asan, C. V. Raman Pillai and Narayana Guru. The city is also known for Sree Padmanabhaswamy Temple, known as the richest temple in the world.[18] The other temples includes the Sreevaraham temple, the Shreekanteswaram temple and the Attukal Bhagavathy temple.
The present regions that constitute Thiruvananthapuram were ruled by the Ays who were related to feudatories of the Chera dynasty.[19] In the 12th century, it was conquered by the Kingdom of Venad.[19] In the 18th century, the king Marthanda Varma expanded the territory, founded the princely state of Travancore and made Thiruvananthapuram its capital.[20] Travancore became the most dominant state in Kerala by defeating the powerful Zamorin of Calicut in the battle of Purakkad in 1755.[21] Following India's independence in 1947, Thiruvananthapuram became the capital of Travancore–Cochin state and remained so until the new Indian state of Kerala was formed in 1956.[22][23]
texts.4:
Thiruvananthapuram is a notable academic and research hub and home to the University of Kerala, APJ Abdul Kalam Technological University, the regional headquarters of Indira Gandhi National Open University, and many other schools and colleges. Thiruvananthapuram is also home to research centres such as the National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology, the Indian Space Research Organisation's Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre, the Indian Institute of Space Science and Technology, the National Centre for Earth Science Studies and a campus of the Indian Institutes of Science Education and Research.[24] Thiruvananthapuram is where India's space programme began, with the headquarters of Liquid Propulsion Systems Centre located there. The city is home to media institutions like Toonz Animation India and Tata Elxsi Ltd, and also to Chitranjali Film Studio, one of the first film studios in Malayalam Cinema, and Kinfra Film and Video Park at Kazhakoottam, which is India's first infotainment industrial park.[25]
In 2012, Thiruvananthapuram was named the best Kerala city to live in, by a field survey conducted by The Times of India.[26] In 2013, the city was ranked the fifteenth best city to live in in India, in a survey conducted by India Today.[27] Thiruvananthapuram was ranked the best Indian city for two consecutive years, 2015 and 2016, according to the Annual Survey of India's City-Systems (ASICS) conducted by the Janaagraha Centre for Citizenship and Democracy.[28] The city was also selected as the best governed city in India in a survey conducted by Janaagraha Centre for citizenship and democracy in 2017.[29]
Etymologyedit
texts.5:
The city takes its name from the Malayalam word thiru-anantha-puram (തിരുവനന്തപുരം [t̪iɾuʋɐnɐn̪d̪ɐpuɾɐm] ⓘ), meaning "The City of Lord Anantha (means infinite, endless, or eternal)",[30] referring to the deity of the Sri Padmanabhaswamy Temple located in the city. Thiruvananthapuram is also known in literature, and popular reference as Ananthapuri, derived from the Sanskrit word Syanandurapuram, meaning "The City of Bliss" in Carnatic kirtanas composed by Swathi Thirunal, erstwhile Maharaja of Travancore.[31] The city was officially referred to as Trivandrum until 1991 (Trivandrum being the anglicised name of the town), when the government decided to reinstate the city's original name Thiruvananthapuram. Many Malayalees still refer to the city as Trivandrum, however.[32] The city was also called as Anandapatnam or Anandapatam in Tamil and Telugu, meaning "The City of Ananda" which has the same meaning as the original name.
